Bearers
bare'erz
n. pl. (porters, carriers of loads; the seventy thousand of Solomon's levy, and the men whose strength Nehemiah reports as decayed)
From bear — Old English beran, to carry — with the agent ending. The Hebrew phrase in every occurrence is nose sabbal or sabbalim, bearers of burdens; the root sabal means to load or carry a heavy thing.

Biblical Definition

The bearers of burdens are the unnamed men whose labour stands behind every building project in Scripture. Solomon's levy: “he set threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work” (2 Chronicles 2:18). Josiah's repair of the house is organised the same way, with Levites “over the bearers of burdens… and overseers of all that wrought the work in any manner of service” (2 Chronicles 34:13). Then Nehemiah records the sentence that every man who has laboured a long time at a hard work recognises: “And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall” (Nehemiah 4:10). Three things at once — the workers are spent, the debris is greater than expected, and the conclusion drawn is that the work cannot be finished. It is the exact midpoint of the book, and it comes with the enemy massing outside. Nehemiah's answer was not a speech about morale but a redeployment: half at the work, half with weapons, and every builder with his sword girded.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a bearer as one who bears, carries or conveys, and one who sustains or supports.

expand to see more

BEARER, n. One who bears, sustains, or carries; a carrier, especially of a corpse to the grave.

2. One who wears any thing; as the bearer of a sword.

3. A tree or plant that yields its fruit; as a good bearer.

BEAR, v.t. To support; to sustain; as, to bear a weight or burden.

BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load.

Key Scripture

2 Chronicles 2:18 — "And he set threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work."

2 Chronicles 34:13 — "Also they were over the bearers of burdens, and were overseers of all that wrought the work in any manner of service: and of the Levites there were scribes, and officers, and porters."

Nehemiah 4:10 — "And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall."

Galatians 6:2 — "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."

Modern Corruption

Ministry exhaustion is treated as a personal failure of resilience, when Nehemiah 4:10 records it as a corporate and structural condition.

expand to see more

When workers give out, the modern instinct is to address the worker — his habits, his boundaries, his capacity. Nehemiah 4:10 does not read that way. The report is corporate (Judah said), the causes are external as well as internal (strength decayed and much rubbish), and the conclusion reached is doctrinal despair (we are not able). Nehemiah responds to all three. He does not deny the fatigue, he does not lecture the men, and he does not simply exhort them to try harder; he reorganises the work so that half stand guard while half build, and he sets families together at the portion of wall nearest their own houses. The remedy is structural, and it is also spiritual: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture names the labourers. Seventy thousand bearers of burdens are recorded in the account of Solomon's temple, and not one of them is named individually; the Chronicler counted them anyway. Every visible work rests on invisible carrying, and Paul makes the same carrying a law of the church: bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. Where that command is obeyed, the strength of the bearers is renewed by distribution rather than exhortation, which is precisely what Nehemiah did with a trowel in one hand and a weapon in the other.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sabbal, a burden-bearer — 2 Chronicles 2:18, Nehemiah 4:10; sabal, to bear a load; massa, a burden; Greek baros, weight — Galatians 6:2.

expand to see more

Hebrew sabbal — a burden-bearer, porter; 2 Chronicles 2:18 and Nehemiah 4:10.

Hebrew sabal — to carry a heavy load; the verb used of the Servant bearing iniquities in Isaiah 53:11.

Hebrew massa — a burden, and also an oracle or prophetic weight.

Hebrew koach — strength; Nehemiah 4:10, “the strength of the bearers… is decayed.”

Greek baros — weight, burden; Galatians 6:2, the burdens the church is to carry for one another.

Usage

"“Threescore and ten thousand… bearers of burdens” — counted though unnamed."

"“The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish” — fatigue and debris together."

"“Bear ye one another's burdens” — the same carrying made a law of the church."
